thread_title: Rare S. purp. venosa Tattnall Co, GA
breadcrumb: Rare S. purp. venosa Tattnall Co, GA

posts.body_html:
Here are some seedlings from S. purpurea ssp. venosa that is supposedly from their southern most coastal plain range in Georgia. What's peculiar about these seedlings is their very close resemblance to S. montana-notice how the hood is recurved in some of the individuals. Could this be an intermediate between venosa and var. montana?


Quite frankly, who knows, but once they get bigger, we'll probably be able to get a better guess at what's going on. Unfortunately, these plants aren't very fast growing...in fact, they're painfully slow to grow, but I still have very high hopes for them!

I bet these are going to look amazing when they grow up-just look at the greenish-yellow background colors, and red veins:



Another shot of the same seedlings:

And here they are, less than a year later from the pics above. They struggled in the beginning of the year, but are growing very fast and gaining momentum now that they're established. They definitely look a bit different from the north and south carolina venosas-maybe the shape is a bit peculiar and unique. Check out how some of them are doing the whole "montana" thing with the hood:








Just to digress a bit, to the left front of the photo is S. purpurea ssp. purupurea from Caroline Co, VA, and behind that are Antho-free S. psittacinas. Georgia venosas are in the middle:

posts.body_html:
Hi Mike:

I've been to the coastal Georgia S. purpurea site and they are no different from Carolina coastal populations. I don't agree with the subspecies construct either since it's not supported by statistical morphological studies on stated subspecies characteristics nor in most genetic studies (mine included). The montane populations, however, can be differentiated.

Your plants looked a little odd, particularly as juveniles. Did you have authentication of provenance and guarantees the group was not contaminated with another genotype (a common problem with Sarracenia growers)?

Sincerely,

Phil Sheridan
Meadowview

Hey Phil,

You are absolutely right to indicate that the two subspecies are not supported by field research/morphological data.
Here is an article that analyzes the situation:
www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/ellisonetal2004ajb.pdf
And again, you are correct to state that the division of S rosea from purpurea is supported.

With that in mind, Mike's purpureas from various localities is a collection. I have 2 quarters from 1962 (silver), one has a D mint and the other is a P mint. both are worth the same, and are from the same year, but just having one doesn't complete the collection.

Whether the populations are genetically different or not doesn't matter much in this situation. Mikes location data, in my mind, is just placed on the label to show where the plants came from.

While the subspecies for purpurea aren't supported by much data, I use the designation to know if this is a northern purpurea or one from a southern state. It might not make a difference genetically, but if an actual county or state can't be given, it is just cool to know where the plant came from, in general.

If anyone has not read Gotelli's article on morphological variation of S. purpurea, I highly recommend it. He is one of the best ecological researchers studying purpurea in the U.S. currently. He also figured out how nitrogen deposition can lead to purpurea producing more phylodes, and possible extinction:
www.uvm.edu/~ngotelli/manuscriptpdfs/Ecology83p2758.pdf

posts.body_html: Phil-I completely missed your inquiry! I understand that the population these came from also have S. flava and S. minor there, and there are hybrids between minor and purpurea and flava and purpurea.  There was also an unusually large minor found there as well.   It's quite possible that historically (many generations ago), these southern purps have  mixed with one or other species, which may account for their "weird" yet amazing appearance.  However, at this point, perhaps they are so back-crossed that it's tough to prove their history without genetic analysis.
